What conclusion follows, then? What image have I brought to your mind?”

My skin crawled as Dupin asked the question. “A madman did this,” I said. “Some raving lunatic who escaped from a nearby psychiatric institution.”

“In certain respects,” he replied, “your suggestion is relevant. But the voices of madmen, even in their most violent fits, never resemble that peculiar voice heard on the stairs. Madmen belong to some nation, and however incoherent their words, their speech still has a recognizable pattern of syllables. Besides, a madman's hair does not look like this hair in my hand. I removed this small tuft from Madame L'Espanaye's tightly clenched fingers. Tell me what you make of it.”

“Dupin!” I exclaimed, completely shaken. “This hair is extraordinarily strange. It isn't human.”

“I haven't claimed that it is,” he said. “But before we settle that point, look at this small sketch I've drawn. It reproduces exactly the marks on Mademoiselle L'Espanaye's throat described in one part of the testimony as dark bruises and deep fingernail impressions, and elsewhere, by Messrs. Dumas and Etienne, as a series of discolored spots evidently left by fingers.

“You'll notice,” my friend continued, spreading the paper on the table before us, “that the drawing suggests a firm, unchanging grip. There is no sign of slipping. Each finger maintained the terrible hold in which it first dug into the flesh, possibly until the victim died. Now try to fit all your fingers into their corresponding impressions at the same time.”

I tried, without success.

“Perhaps we're not testing this fairly,” he said. “The paper lies on a flat surface, whereas the human neck is cylindrical. Here's a piece of wood with roughly the same circumference as the throat. Wrap the drawing around it and try again.”

I followed his instructions, but the difficulty was even clearer. “This,” I said, “isn't the mark of a human hand.”

“Now read this passage from Cuvier,” Dupin replied.

It was a detailed anatomical and general description of the large, tawny orangutan of the East Indian Islands. Everyone is sufficiently familiar with these mammals' gigantic size, tremendous strength and agility, savage ferocity, and tendency to imitate. At once I understood the full horror of the murder.

“The description of the fingers,” I said when I finished reading, “matches this drawing exactly.

I thanked him and apologized. He said, “Not at all,” and continued.

“Miss Havisham was now an heiress and, as you can imagine, much sought after as an excellent marriage prospect. Her half brother once again had substantial means, but debts and fresh extravagance led him to squander them terribly. The hostility between brother and sister was greater than it had been between him and his father. People suspect that he nursed a deep, deadly resentment towards her, believing she had encouraged his father's anger. Now I come to the cruel part of the story—pausing only, my dear Handel, to observe that a dinner napkin will not fit inside a drinking glass.”

I cannot explain why I was trying to stuff mine into my glass. All I know is that I found myself struggling desperately to compress it into that space, with a persistence worthy of a far better purpose. Again I thanked him and apologized. Again he replied with the utmost cheerfulness, “Not at all, really!” and went on.

“A certain man appeared on the scene—at the races, public dances, or wherever you please—and began courting Miss Havisham. I never saw him, since all this happened twenty-five years ago, before either of us was born, Handel. But I've heard my father say that he was a flashy fellow and just the sort for such an undertaking. My father emphatically insists, though, that only ignorance or prejudice could have allowed anyone to mistake him for a gentleman. He holds that no man who wasn't a true gentleman at heart has ever, since the world began, been a true gentleman in his manners. No varnish can hide the grain of wood, he says; the more varnish you apply, the more clearly the grain shows. Well, this man pursued Miss Havisham persistently and claimed to be devoted to her. I understand she had shown little susceptibility to love before then, but every bit she possessed certainly emerged at that point. She loved him passionately. There's no doubt that she absolutely worshipped him. He exploited her affection so systematically that he obtained large sums of money from her. He also persuaded her to buy out her brother's share of the brewery, which their father had weakly left him, for an enormous price. His excuse was that, once they married, he would need to own and manage the whole business. Your guardian wasn't advising Miss Havisham at that time, and she was too proud and too much in love to take advice from anyone.

I passed several funerals, each with few mourners. Onlookers regarded them as signs of the gravest danger. Some watched the processions with feverish eagerness; others hurried away in fear; some wept aloud.

After the immediate relief of the sick, Adrian's principal concern had been to conceal the plague's symptoms and spread from London's inhabitants. He knew that fear and gloomy anticipation strengthened disease, and that despair and anxious brooding made the human body especially vulnerable to infection. Consequently, no distressing spectacles were visible. Most shops remained open, and the movement of pedestrians continued to some extent. Yet although the appearance of a stricken city had been avoided, London looked greatly changed to me, since I had not seen it since the outbreak began. There were no carriages, and tall grass grew in the streets. The houses looked abandoned, with most shutters closed. The people I met wore a ghastly, frightened stare, very different from Londoners' usual businesslike manner. My solitary carriage drew attention as it rattled towards the Protectoral Palace. The fashionable streets approaching it looked more desolate and deserted still. Adrian's antechamber was crowded; this was the hour when he received visitors. Unwilling to interrupt his work, I waited, watching the petitioners arrive and depart. They belonged to the middle and lower classes, whose livelihoods had disappeared with the collapse of trade and the busy pursuit of profit that pervaded every branch of life in our country. New arrivals looked anxious, sometimes terrified, in marked contrast to the resigned, even satisfied expressions of those who had been heard. I recognized my friend's influence in their livelier movements and cheerful faces. When the clock struck two, no more were admitted. Those who had missed their chance left sullenly or sorrowfully, while I entered the audience chamber.

The improvement in Adrian's health struck me immediately. He no longer drooped towards the ground like an over-tended spring flower that has grown beyond its strength and bends beneath the weight of its own blossoms. His eyes shone, his expression was composed, and his entire bearing conveyed a concentrated energy very unlike his former weariness. He sat at a table with several secretaries, who sorted petitions or recorded the notes made during that day's audience. Two or three petitioners were still waiting. I admired his fairness and patience. Those who could support themselves outside London he advised to leave immediately, providing them with the means to do so.
